question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20(a), where must a broker who receives money or other property belonging to another person in a real estate transaction maintain those funds?
choice_a: In a separate, federally insured trust or escrow account at a financial institution in Georgia, designated as such
choice_b: In the broker's general operating account, clearly labeled
choice_c: In a personal savings account in the broker's name
choice_d: Georgia law imposes no specific institutional or insurance requirement
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-20(a) requires a broker who accepts trust funds to maintain a separate, federally insured trust or escrow account at a Georgia financial institution.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, when a licensee who does not otherwise maintain a trust or escrow account receives trust funds for the first time, by when must the funds be deposited into a properly designated trust account?
choice_a: Not later than one business day after receipt
choice_b: Within 10 calendar days
choice_c: By the end of the same calendar month
choice_d: There is no fixed deadline, only a general 'reasonable time' standard
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-20 requires a licensee who does not already maintain a trust account and who receives trust funds for the first time to deposit them not later than one business day after receipt.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, which of the following must a broker place into the properly designated trust or escrow account, rather than commingling with personal or business funds?
choice_a: All down payments, earnest money deposits, and other trust funds received on behalf of another person
choice_b: Only funds exceeding $1,000
choice_c: Only funds from commercial transactions
choice_d: Only funds received directly from a lender
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-20 requires all down payments, earnest money deposits, and other trust funds received on behalf of another to go into the designated trust account, prohibiting commingling.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, a broker's trust or escrow account that is properly established and registered with the Commission is protected from what?
choice_a: Attachment or garnishment by the broker's own creditors
choice_b: Any examination by the Commission
choice_c: State income taxation
choice_d: Federal deposit insurance limits
explanation: A properly registered trust account is protected from attachment or garnishment by the broker's own creditors, since the funds belong to the parties to the transaction, not the broker.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, aside from its mandatory renewal-period examination, when else may the Commission examine a broker's trust account records?
choice_a: At any time upon reasonable cause
choice_b: Only pursuant to a court order
choice_c: Only if a written consumer complaint has been filed
choice_d: The Commission may never examine trust records outside the renewal period
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-20 authorizes the Commission to examine a broker's trust account records at any time upon reasonable cause, in addition to its mandatory examination during each renewal period.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, how often, at minimum, must the Commission examine a broker's trust or escrow account records?
choice_a: During each license renewal period
choice_b: Only once, at initial licensure
choice_c: Every ten years
choice_d: Only upon the broker's voluntary request
explanation: The Commission must examine a broker's trust account records during each renewal period, and may also examine them at other times upon reasonable cause.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, what may a broker submit in lieu of a direct Commission examination of trust account records?
choice_a: A report prepared by a certified public accountant
choice_b: A notarized personal affidavit from the broker
choice_c: A letter from the broker's attorney
choice_d: Nothing -- direct examination can never be substituted
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-20 allows a broker to submit a certified public accountant's report as an alternative to a direct Commission examination of trust account records.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, when does a broker become entitled to disburse trust funds such as earnest money to himself or herself as commission?
choice_a: Only after the transaction has been consummated or terminated
choice_b: As soon as the earnest money is deposited
choice_c: At the broker's discretion, once the listing agreement is signed
choice_d: Only with the buyer's verbal permission
explanation: A broker is not entitled to earnest money or other trust funds as commission until the transaction has been consummated or terminated.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), before a broker may deposit trust funds into an interest-bearing account, what must first exist?
choice_a: A written agreement of the interested parties consenting to the interest-bearing arrangement
choice_b: Verbal consent of the buyer only
choice_c: Prior Commission approval of the specific financial institution
choice_d: Nothing -- a broker may place trust funds in an interest-bearing account at any time without consent
explanation: Depositing trust funds in an interest-bearing account without first obtaining the interested parties' written consent is listed among the unfair trade practices in O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b).

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, may a broker maintain more than one designated trust or escrow account?
choice_a: Yes, a broker may maintain multiple trust accounts provided the Commission is properly notified
choice_b: No, Georgia law limits each broker to a single trust account
choice_c: Only with special Commission dispensation granted case-by-case at a hearing
choice_d: Only if each account is held at a different out-of-state institution
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-20 permits a broker to maintain multiple designated trust accounts, provided the Commission is properly notified of each.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-20, what accommodation does Georgia law make for a nonresident broker regarding the location of a required trust account?
choice_a: A nonresident broker may maintain the trust account at a financial institution in the broker's home state
choice_b: Nonresident brokers are exempt from the trust account requirement entirely
choice_c: A nonresident broker must use a Georgia-based national bank only
choice_d: Nonresident brokers must deposit all trust funds directly with the Commission
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-20 allows a nonresident broker to maintain the required trust account at a financial institution located in the broker's home state.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), which of the following is listed as an unfair trade practice subjecting a licensee to Commission discipline?
choice_a: Commingling trust funds with the broker's own funds, or failing to maintain a required trust account
choice_b: Charging a commission rate higher than the local market average
choice_c: Representing a client in more than one simultaneous transaction
choice_d: Advertising a property using its correct legal description
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) lists commingling trust funds and failing to maintain a required trust account among the enumerated unfair trade practices subjecting a licensee to discipline.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), an affiliated licensee (associate broker or salesperson) who receives trust funds on behalf of a client has what specific duty regarding those funds?
choice_a: To promptly deposit or turn over the funds to the broker or into the properly designated trust account, rather than holding them personally
choice_b: No specific duty -- only the broker who signs the listing bears responsibility
choice_c: A duty to invest the funds on the client's behalf pending closing
choice_d: A duty to deposit the funds within 30 days
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) lists an associate broker's or salesperson's failure to promptly deposit or turn over trust funds received on a client's behalf as a prohibited unfair trade practice.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), within how many days after a listing expires or is withdrawn must a licensee remove any 'for sale,' 'for rent,' or similar sign from the property, absent the owner's authorization to leave it?
choice_a: 10 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_c: 5 days
choice_d: 60 days
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) requires removal of a sign within 10 days after a listing expires or is withdrawn unless the owner has authorized it to remain.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), engaging in intentionally false or misleading advertising is classified as what?
choice_a: An unfair trade practice subjecting the licensee to Commission sanction
choice_b: A civil matter only, outside the Commission's jurisdiction
choice_c: Permissible so long as no consumer files a complaint
choice_d: A violation only if the advertisement appears in print media
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) lists intentionally advertising material that is misleading or inaccurate as a prohibited unfair trade practice.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), may a licensee advertise or represent to a buyer that a property will increase in value or can be resold at a profit?
choice_a: No, guaranteeing a future resale profit is listed as a prohibited unfair trade practice
choice_b: Yes, provided the representation is made in good faith
choice_c: Yes, but only for investment or commercial property
choice_d: Yes, if the licensee has at least five years of experience
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) prohibits guaranteeing future resale profits as an unfair trade practice, regardless of the licensee's good faith or experience.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a real estate licensee who is not a licensed appraiser may prepare a comparative market analysis or opinion of value, but is prohibited from doing what?
choice_a: Calling that opinion an 'appraisal'
choice_b: Charging any fee for the opinion
choice_c: Sharing the opinion with the client in writing
choice_d: Basing the opinion on comparable sales
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) prohibits an unlicensed appraiser from calling a value opinion an 'appraisal,' even though preparing the opinion itself is permitted.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), what must a licensee do regarding a fee, rebate, or referral compensation received in connection with the transaction, such as from a lender, attorney, or inspector?
choice_a: Disclose it; non-disclosure of such fees or referral compensation to the principal is listed as a prohibited unfair trade practice
choice_b: Nothing -- referral fees need not be disclosed to anyone
choice_c: Deposit the referral fee into the trust account
choice_d: Split the referral fee equally with the client
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) requires disclosure of fees, rebates, and referral compensation to the principal; failing to disclose them is a prohibited unfair trade practice.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), may an affiliated licensee accept a real estate commission or fee directly from a source other than the licensee's own employing broker?
choice_a: No, accepting compensation from anyone other than the licensee's own broker for licensed activity is a prohibited unfair trade practice
choice_b: Yes, as long as the licensee later reports the payment
choice_c: Yes, if the payment is under $500
choice_d: Yes, provided the client consents
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) prohibits an affiliated licensee from accepting compensation for licensed activity from any source other than the licensee's own employing broker.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee acting in a dual capacity -- for example, as both agent and an undisclosed principal in the same transaction -- without proper disclosure has committed what?
choice_a: A prohibited unfair trade practice
choice_b: A permitted practice, since the licensee already knows the property
choice_c: A practice requiring only after-the-fact notice to the Commission
choice_d: A practice allowed if the transaction is for the licensee's own primary residence
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) lists acting as both agent and an undisclosed principal, without proper disclosure, as a prohibited unfair trade practice.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee who induces a party to breach an existing, valid brokerage engagement with another broker in order to substitute a new agreement has committed what?
choice_a: A prohibited unfair trade practice
choice_b: Permissible competitive solicitation
choice_c: A violation only if done in writing
choice_d: A violation only if the other broker consents
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) prohibits inducing a party to breach an existing brokerage engagement in order to substitute a new one.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), if a property is subject to another broker's exclusive brokerage engagement, is a licensee generally permitted to negotiate directly with the owner without going through the listing broker?
choice_a: No, negotiating directly with a party known to be subject to another broker's exclusive engagement is a prohibited unfair trade practice, subject to limited exceptions
choice_b: Yes, provided the licensee has a ready buyer
choice_c: Yes, as long as the licensee discloses the contact afterward
choice_d: Yes, if more than 30 days have passed since the listing began
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) generally prohibits negotiating directly with a party known to be subject to another broker's exclusive brokerage engagement, subject to limited statutory exceptions.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a Georgia licensee who practices real estate brokerage in another state without holding a license valid in that state has committed what?
choice_a: A prohibited unfair trade practice under Georgia law
choice_b: No violation, since Georgia law only governs conduct occurring within Georgia
choice_c: A violation only if the other state formally complains to the Commission
choice_d: A minor infraction exempt from Commission sanction
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) treats practicing real estate brokerage in another state without a valid license there as a prohibited unfair trade practice under Georgia law.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), may a broker pay a real estate commission to a person who does not hold a real estate license?
choice_a: Generally no, except within narrow statutory carve-outs (such as for the estate of a deceased licensee or certain foreign referral agents)
choice_b: Yes, without any restriction
choice_c: Yes, but only for referrals from out-of-state buyers
choice_d: Yes, if the unlicensed person is a family member of the client
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) generally prohibits paying commissions to unlicensed persons, subject to narrow statutory exceptions such as a deceased licensee's estate or certain foreign referral arrangements.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee who files a document creating a false lien or cloud on a property's title, based on an invalid claim of a listing agreement, has committed what?
choice_a: A prohibited unfair trade practice
choice_b: A permissible method of enforcing an unpaid commission claim
choice_c: A civil filing outside the Commission's jurisdiction
choice_d: A violation only if the claim exceeds $5,000
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) prohibits filing a document that creates a false lien or cloud on title based on an invalid claim of a listing agreement.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), may a licensee induce another party to alter or interfere with another licensee's earned compensation without that licensee's consent?
choice_a: No, doing so is listed as a prohibited unfair trade practice
choice_b: Yes, if the inducing licensee represents the buyer
choice_c: Yes, as long as it happens after closing
choice_d: Yes, provided the client requests it
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) prohibits inducing another party to alter or interfere with another licensee's earned compensation without that licensee's consent.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), failing to timely make the required written disclosure of an agency relationship is classified as what?
choice_a: A prohibited unfair trade practice subjecting the licensee to Commission discipline
choice_b: A purely administrative oversight with no disciplinary consequence
choice_c: A violation only if the client demands rescission
choice_d: A violation only in dual agency transactions, not single agency
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) lists failure to timely disclose an agency relationship as a prohibited unfair trade practice.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-3, how is a 'client' defined?
choice_a: A person being represented by a real estate broker in an agency capacity pursuant to a brokerage engagement
choice_b: Any person who contacts a licensee about a property, regardless of representation
choice_c: A person who has signed a purchase agreement
choice_d: A person receiving only ministerial assistance from a broker
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-3 defines a 'client' as a person represented by a broker in an agency capacity under a brokerage engagement.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-3, how is a 'customer' defined?
choice_a: A person who is not being represented by a real estate broker in an agency capacity, though the broker may still provide ministerial services
choice_b: A person who has signed a brokerage engagement with the broker
choice_c: A person who has paid the broker a retainer
choice_d: Any licensee affiliated with the broker's firm
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-3 defines a 'customer' as someone not represented by the broker in an agency capacity, distinguishing that person from a 'client.'

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-3, a 'dual agent' is defined as a broker who does what?
choice_a: Simultaneously has a client relationship with both the seller and buyer, or both the landlord and tenant, in the same transaction
choice_b: Holds real estate licenses in two different states
choice_c: Represents two unrelated sellers in two unrelated transactions
choice_d: Works for two different brokerage firms at the same time
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-3 defines a 'dual agent' as a broker who simultaneously has a client relationship with both parties to the same transaction.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-3, a 'designated agent' is defined as what?
choice_a: One or more licensees affiliated with a broker who are assigned by the broker to represent solely one client in a transaction
choice_b: A licensee who has passed a Commission-administered designation exam
choice_c: The broker's chosen successor upon retirement
choice_d: A licensee designated to handle only commercial transactions
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-3 defines a 'designated agent' as one or more licensees assigned by the broker to represent solely one client in a transaction.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-4(a), what standard of duty does a Georgia broker owe a client absent an express written agreement providing otherwise?
choice_a: Only the statutory duties set out in the chapter, performed with reasonable care -- not full common-law fiduciary duty
choice_b: Full common-law fiduciary duty automatically, as in most other states
choice_c: No duty whatsoever unless separately negotiated
choice_d: Only the duties owed to a customer, never a client
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-4(a) displaces common-law fiduciary duty by default, limiting a broker's duty to the statutory obligations performed with reasonable care, unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-4(a), may a broker and client expand the broker's duties beyond the statutory minimum?
choice_a: Yes, but only by express agreement in a writing signed by the parties
choice_b: No, the statutory duties are a fixed ceiling that cannot be altered
choice_c: Yes, through a verbal side agreement
choice_d: Yes, automatically once the client requests it
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-4(a) allows broker duties to be expanded beyond the statutory minimum only by express written agreement signed by the parties.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-4(b), if a broker already has an existing brokerage relationship with a party and enters into a new brokerage engagement involving that same party, what must the broker do?
choice_a: Timely disclose that fact and the new brokerage relationship to all brokers, customers, or clients involved in the transaction
choice_b: Nothing, since the parties already know each other
choice_c: Terminate the earlier relationship before proceeding
choice_d: Obtain Commission pre-approval before entering the new engagement
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-4(b) requires a broker to timely disclose an existing relationship with a party to all brokers, customers, or clients in a new, related transaction.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5(a), a broker engaged by a seller must present offers to the seller how?
choice_a: Timely -- promptly presenting all offers and counteroffers, even while other offers are pending
choice_b: Only offers at or above the listed price
choice_c: Only after the listing period ends
choice_d: Only if requested in writing by the seller
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5(a) requires a seller's broker to timely present all offers and counteroffers to the seller, regardless of other pending offers.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5(b), a seller's broker must timely disclose to prospective buyers what kind of facts about the property, even though the broker represents the seller?
choice_a: Adverse material facts about the property's physical condition, including defects and environmental contamination, that would not be discovered by a reasonably diligent inspection
choice_b: Every fact the seller has ever mentioned about the property, regardless of materiality
choice_c: Only facts that are already listed on the seller's disclosure statement
choice_d: Nothing -- a seller's broker owes buyers no disclosure duty whatsoever
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5(b) requires a seller's broker to timely disclose adverse material facts about the property's physical condition, including defects and environmental contamination not discoverable by reasonable inspection.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5(b), a seller's broker must disclose material facts about adverse conditions within what distance of the property, if actually known to the broker?
choice_a: Within one mile of the property
choice_b: Within the same subdivision only, regardless of distance
choice_c: Within the same county
choice_d: There is no distance limitation -- all known adverse conditions citywide must be disclosed
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5(b) requires disclosure of material facts about adverse conditions within one mile of the property, if actually known to the broker.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5, if a matter is not among the facts a broker is statutorily required to disclose, when is the broker liable for failing to disclose it?
choice_a: Only if the failure amounts to fraud -- the statute creates no independent duty to discover or disclose non-enumerated matters
choice_b: Whenever a buyer later claims harm, regardless of the broker's knowledge
choice_c: Whenever the fact would have been material to a reasonable buyer
choice_d: The broker is strictly liable for any undisclosed defect
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5 limits broker liability for non-enumerated disclosure matters to cases of fraud, creating no independent duty to discover or disclose beyond the statute's list.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5, does a seller's broker breach any duty to the seller merely by showing other properties to other prospective buyers, including buyers interested in the seller's own listing?
choice_a: No, showing alternative properties to other buyers does not, by itself, breach the broker's duty to the seller
choice_b: Yes, this is an automatic breach of the duty of loyalty
choice_c: Yes, unless the seller pre-approves each showing in writing
choice_d: This only breaches the duty if the other property is listed by the same firm
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5 confirms that a broker does not breach the duty owed to a seller merely by showing other properties to other buyers.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-6, the duties a broker owes to a landlord-client -- including seeking acceptable lease terms and timely presenting all offers -- most closely parallel the duties owed to what other type of client under the Act?
choice_a: A seller-client under O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5
choice_b: A buyer-client under O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7
choice_c: A customer receiving only ministerial services
choice_d: A dual agent's clients under O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-6's landlord-broker duties parallel the seller-broker duty structure of O.C.G.A. 10-6A-5, including timely presentation of offers and disclosure of adverse material facts.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7(a), if a matter in a transaction is beyond the buyer's broker's expertise, what must the broker do?
choice_a: Recommend that the buyer obtain expert consultation on that matter
choice_b: Resolve the matter personally regardless of expertise
choice_c: Ignore the matter unless the buyer specifically raises it
choice_d: Refer the buyer to the seller's broker for an opinion
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7(a) requires a buyer's broker to recommend that the buyer obtain expert consultation on matters beyond the broker's expertise.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7(a), under what condition must a buyer's broker keep information received from the buyer confidential?
choice_a: When the buyer has made an express request that the information be kept confidential, subject to limited statutory exceptions
choice_b: All buyer information is automatically confidential, with no exceptions
choice_c: Confidentiality applies only after the transaction closes
choice_d: The buyer's broker owes no confidentiality duty at all
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7(a) ties a buyer's broker's confidentiality duty to the buyer's express request, subject to limited statutory exceptions.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7(b), when a transaction involves seller or owner financing, what must a buyer's broker disclose to the seller?
choice_a: Material adverse facts actually known by the broker concerning the buyer's financial ability to complete the transaction, and, for residential property, occupancy intentions
choice_b: The buyer's full credit report, regardless of relevance
choice_c: Nothing -- the buyer's broker owes the seller no disclosure duty
choice_d: Only the buyer's employer, and nothing about finances
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7(b) requires disclosure to the seller of known material adverse facts about the buyer's financial ability and, for residential property, occupancy intentions, when seller or owner financing is involved.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7(c), may a buyer's broker assist an unrepresented seller with ministerial acts, such as preparing a form contract, without thereby creating a brokerage relationship with that seller?
choice_a: Yes, ministerial assistance to a seller does not, by itself, create a brokerage relationship
choice_b: No, any assistance to a seller automatically creates a client relationship
choice_c: Only if the seller pays a separate fee for the assistance
choice_d: Only with prior written Commission approval
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-7(c) confirms that a buyer's broker may perform ministerial acts for a seller without creating a brokerage relationship with that seller.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-9(a), absent a different term specified in the brokerage engagement, how long does a broker-client relationship continue after it commences?
choice_a: Until completion, expiration, or termination of the engagement, or one year, whichever occurs first
choice_b: Indefinitely, until either party affirmatively cancels it
choice_c: A fixed 90 days regardless of the engagement's terms
choice_d: Until the broker's license next comes up for renewal
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-9(a) provides that a broker-client relationship continues until completion, expiration, or termination of the engagement, or one year, whichever comes first, absent a different specified term.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-9(b), what duties does a broker continue to owe a client after the brokerage relationship has terminated?
choice_a: Limited duties to account for funds or property and to maintain confidentiality, subject to certain exceptions
choice_b: No duties whatsoever survive termination
choice_c: The full statutory duty list continues indefinitely
choice_d: Only a duty to refer the former client to a new broker
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-9(b) limits post-termination duties to accounting for funds or property and maintaining confidentiality, subject to statutory exceptions.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-9(c), if a broker's duty of confidentiality to a client would conflict with the broker's duty not to give customers false information, which duty prevails?
choice_a: The duty not to give false information to customers prevails
choice_b: Confidentiality always prevails over any competing duty
choice_c: The broker must resolve the conflict by withdrawing from the transaction entirely
choice_d: Whichever duty the broker's client instructs the broker to follow
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-9(c) provides that the broker's duty not to give customers false information prevails over the confidentiality duty owed to a client.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12, under what condition may a broker act as a dual agent representing both parties to a transaction?
choice_a: Only with the written, informed consent of both clients, obtained through a document containing statutorily enumerated disclosures
choice_b: Automatically, whenever the broker represents both the buyer and seller
choice_c: With verbal consent from at least one of the two clients
choice_d: Dual agency is categorically prohibited in Georgia under all circumstances
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12 permits dual agency only with the written, informed consent of both clients, using a document containing the statute's enumerated disclosures.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12, the required dual agency consent document must include a statement of what?
choice_a: That the client does not have to consent to the dual agency
choice_b: That the client waives all rights to sue the broker
choice_c: That the broker will receive a reduced commission
choice_d: That the transaction will close within 30 days
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12 requires the dual agency consent document to state that the client does not have to consent to the dual agency.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12, once a client has signed the required dual agency consent document, how is that consent treated, and what happens to knowledge held by the dual agent regarding each client?
choice_a: The consent is conclusively deemed informed, and knowledge is not imputed between the two clients
choice_b: The consent may still be challenged as uninformed at any time before closing
choice_c: Everything one client tells the dual agent is automatically imputed to the other client
choice_d: The consent must be re-signed at every stage of the transaction
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12 treats a signed dual agency consent as conclusively informed and prevents imputation of one client's knowledge to the other.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-13(a), how may a broker use designated agency to handle a transaction involving both a buyer-client and a seller-client of the same firm?
choice_a: By assigning different affiliated licensees as designated agents, each representing only one client, under a company policy reasonably calculated to ensure proper representation
choice_b: By requiring the same licensee to represent both parties as a dual agent in every instance
choice_c: Designated agency is not recognized under Georgia law
choice_d: By having the broker personally represent only the higher-commission side
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-13(a) allows a broker to assign different affiliated licensees as designated agents, each representing only one client in the same transaction, under a proper company policy.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-13(b), when a broker properly appoints separate designated agents for the buyer and seller in the same transaction, are the broker, the licensees, or the firm deemed dual agents?
choice_a: No, none of them is deemed to be a dual agent
choice_b: Yes, the broker is automatically deemed a dual agent
choice_c: Yes, both designated agents are individually deemed dual agents
choice_d: Only the firm, not the individual licensees, is deemed a dual agent
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-13(b) provides that neither the broker, the licensees, nor the firm is deemed a dual agent when separate designated agents are properly appointed.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-13(c), in a designated agency arrangement, is confidential information known by one designated agent automatically imputed to the other designated agent or to the broker?
choice_a: No, each designated agent is deemed to possess only that agent's own actual knowledge, and confidential information is not disclosed except as the statute allows
choice_b: Yes, all designated agents and the broker are treated as possessing identical knowledge
choice_c: Only the broker automatically receives all designated agents' confidential information
choice_d: Imputation depends on whether the licensees share the same office
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-13(c) limits each designated agent to that agent's own actual knowledge and restricts disclosure of confidential information, preventing automatic imputation.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-14(a), which of the following is an example of a ministerial act a broker may perform for a customer without creating an agency relationship?
choice_a: Acting as a scribe in the preparation of a real estate form contract
choice_b: Negotiating price on the customer's behalf
choice_c: Advising the customer on an acceptable offer strategy
choice_d: Representing the customer's interests in a dispute with the other party
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-14(a) lists acting as a scribe in preparing a real estate form contract as a ministerial act a broker may perform for a customer without creating an agency relationship.

question: Under BRRETA, O.C.G.A. 10-6A-14(b), even when acting only as a transaction broker for a customer rather than as an agent for a client, what duties must the broker still perform?
choice_a: Timely presenting all offers, accounting for funds received, and disclosing known adverse material facts
choice_b: No duties at all, since a customer is not a client
choice_c: Only the duty to close the transaction on time
choice_d: Only the duty to collect the commission
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-14(b) requires a transaction broker to still timely present offers, account for funds received, and disclose known adverse material facts, even without an agency relationship.
